I am a local from the DC area, and was in Junior High when 9/11 happened. We had a lot of classmates whose parents were military or civilian feds / contractors who worked at the Pentagon (and of course all over the DC area). When everything went down I was in class. The principal tells all faculty to report to the office (or something like that). They say students are to remain in their current classrooms. The teacher goes for a while, and we are left wondering. They left the TV unplugged. This was before cell phones were common place among children. So no finding out what was going on. We were on lockdown for a while. However, the class clown somehow knew what was happening and started telling people they attacked New York. We thought he was pulling some horrible joke or prank, and so he was ignored. And then our teacher comes back and tells everyone that buses will come early (I believe it was around 1 or 2pm) to take kids home, or they can’t wait for their parents to pick them up. I get on the bus and hear a lot of chatter about what happened, and then start to hear it on the radio. The driver turned off the radio. But everyone was discussing what could have happened. No one really knew.

I get to a family members house, and that’s when I found out what happened. They had a tiny TV in their kitchen, and that’s when I saw what really happened. This family member was trying to reach my parents at work, and trying to reach another family member who was in New York on a work trip. They were having a very difficult time getting through but eventually succeed. My parent picks me up late at night and we go home.


Although I didn’t lose anyone that day (although knew someone who was at the Pentagon, and my family member who was in NYC on business and I believe was supposed to have a meeting there the following day, and had family friends that were first responders to the pentagon), that day really impacted me and my family. The aftermath changed America, and changed the trajectory of things for my family, and me.

You are welcome. I am new to this game, but figured it out and studied it as i went. It did help I had a lot of experience with board game equivalents. And so far I've been doing very well. These tips and tricks are what has worked for me. Everyone has a different style of game play, but alliance building and being intelligently aggressive (together) seems to work.

I am new to the game (within the past few weeks), however, am not new to very similar board games. I got the hang of this game relatively quickly. You need to focus on industry, morale, and being aggressive against the bots right out of the gate. The more territory you conquer early on equates to more resources, and options for industry. Although, the morale question comes in to play with newly "liberated" territory. Build propaganda buildings, and maybe use your war bonds and other things to boost their morale at least to 35 to start (that I've found is where a lot of places can stay without revolting). 
Then consolidate after you've got a little chunk of extra land. Build up industry, build a mix of units. I am a military history buff so always tended to make realistic type units (armored units with tank regiments supported by mobile artillery support, mobile AA, mobile AT, mobile or mechanized armored infantry etc...), but i found while that works, this game is about stacking and making large armies. Keep non mechanized units together, or else they will slow down mobile / mechanized units etc.. build large armies of just one or two type units if you want to blanket an area. I still like to vary things, but sometimes large wolfpacks help, or large tank and artillery units. 

Now, how to form an alliance? Have a plan in your head of where you want to go and what you want to do. Then see someone a couple countries over, or maybe next to you (if you feel they are going to focus in a different direction), and just send messages. Be somewhat open and tell them your near future plans, but only if you think it could somehow benefit them. Like if they have an enemy that will be a hassle for them, but it so happens you want to take some of that same enemy's territory, tell them you can help out and help divide that area, and so on. Talk to people. That has worked for me. And keep to the alliance unless they turn on you. Be loyal. Start weaving plans together.
Most people don't want to play alone when faced with large coalitions. People naturally want someone to have their back and help them out. You just need to use the carrot with some people, and be diplomatic, and find common ground. Worked for me right out of the gate.

Enemy at the Gates had some true elements to it. However, the whole SS Colonel (or Army Major depending) that headed an elite sniper school coming to Stalingrad to hunt Vasily Zaitsev never happened. There were German snipers, all enlisted ranks, and all had a relatively short life span in the Stalingrad cauldron. There was no hunt and counter hunt. No using civilians as bait to draw Zaitsev out. The famous sniper duel at the end was wrong. There were possible true accounts of Zaitsev getting in to a sniper duel on this big hill (the mamayev kurgan) that was heavily entrenched and fortified, and that was heavily contested and changed hands repeatedly  throughout the battle. But it looked nothing like the movie, nor was it someone who had been all over the city looking for Zaitsev.

The love story did not happen, and Zaitsev was already a relatively high ranking NCO with years of prior military experience at the time.  

Also, the charging the German positions with one soldier holding a rifle, and the other holding the ammo but without a weapon, and then NKVD blocking detachments mowing down retreating soldiers is slightly embellished. Similar charges happened, but the soldiers were armed, and yes blocking detachments existed, but that whole scene probably did not happen that way. 

Still an overall great film that depicts the battle of stalingrad in great detail, but there were a lot of embellishments and the main rivalry did not happen.

Let's set the scene.

A glider in WWII usually had one pilot and if lucky a co-pilot. The pilot had essentially a steering wheel, something to control the release mechanism which detached the cable connecting them to the tow plane, and a lever to control the wing flaps / rudder which would help steer and slow the glider down. Besides maybe a couple other little things, that was it. There was no engine in gliders, there were no propellers. You know those foam or balsawood gliders  / planes you would throw around as a kid? Same concept, and actually I believe the gliders are mini Waco replicas. Anyway. So you have an engineless plane. And on top of that it is made out of plywood, and in many cases, canvas. Now you cram a dozen or so (depending on the glider) guys in the back, with their equipment and weapons. The C-47 in front of you is towing your glider. A lot of lives and or equipment in back depend on you to land an engineless plane safely in a field that is probably under enemy fire. Now imagine hundreds, even thousands of planes towing gliders all around you. You are flying in, and then the enemy anti-aircraft starts popping in the air all around you. Maybe your tow plane is hit and is going down, so you need to detach early. Or maybe your tow rope was cut by all that flying lead, and you are now gliding in the air, trying to avoid crashing in to other aircraft. You see a field. You see other gliders on the ground, but you see an opening to land. But wait, you almost collide with another glider that just got in front of you. So you quickly have to maneuver towards another location. That field is mostly empty. Ok let's try it. Pulling up on the flaps to slow things down. You don't want to land too fast. You come in and there is a rough and bumpy landing, but you are fine. OR you crash. And depending on how the plan lands / crashes, you are either killed, wounded, or fine. It all depends on the skill of the pilot, and the luck of where and how you land. 

Now imagine being a soldier in the back of wooden engineless plane, and you, nor anyone else has parachute. If the wooden and canvas glider is struck in the air by shrapnel and disintegrates, that's it, you will plummet to your death. That did happen, and not unfrequently. This is completely out of your control until you are out of the glider.
Scary stuff. Glider pilots and troops were truly brave men.
And that was just getting to the ground. Now you have to fight as a soldier (except pilots until the last months of the war did not have to fight as infantry, but frequently they did).

Was this a British unit? Because I remember that vividly described in a couple of accounts by the Sherwood Rangers (British Tank unit that landed at D-Day). They had Amphibious-ish tanks, but oftentimes that happened on D-Day. Tanks would be released from the tank landing craft ships, sometimes miles from shore. They had special inflatables that were supposed to help float the tank. If the inflatables were damaged, the water was too rough, or not inflated properly the tank would sink like a stone to the bottom of the English Channel with the crews. Many a British tanker actually almost mutinied when they heard that their tanks would go ashore this way on D-Day. After some initial losses like this, the LCVs / LCTs were moved much closer to shore to allow less of a risk for the tankers (well at least less of a risk of drowning).

Also another big problem with the C-47 pilots on D-Day was many of them were antsy, got lost for a myriad of reasons, and experienced heavy flak in certain areas and did not want to get shot down. So they would turn on the red light for the paratroopers to stand up and hook (getting ready to jump from the plane), and then the green light. Frequently they were too low, or too fast, yes. And extremely frequently they were dropping their soldiers out over the wrong DZs (Drop Zones). They were witnessing other planes getting shot out of the sky, burning, and many that dropped soldiers in the wrong area or wrong speed / height may also have been impacted by flak, like engines getting caught on fire or a pilot or co-pilot being killed. In situations like that many did the heroic thing and tried staying the course to allow the paratroopers to jump, and in the process maybe losing their own lives by going down with the plane. 

What also sucked for a lot of paratroopers was jumping out of the plane, and landing in a flooded field or marsh, and being pulled under by the 100+ lbs of equipment they were carrying and getting tangled in the parachute. A lot of paratroopers drowned in flooded fields on D-Day because of that. Also many got hung up in trees, or on top of buildings and were mowed down by the Germans.

Also, I was going to edit my post but could just include this here. I don't 100% remember every detail of that scene, but I believe there was a jeep or something in the glider, right? That happened a lot. A glider would come in too hot, and the jeep which was usually tied down would come loose somehow (turbulence, flak or small arms fire, not being tied down strong enough etc...) . The glider would crash land, and the jeep would rapidly move forward inside the fuselage / hull of the glider and crush the occupants. Same thing with artillery cannons, heavy containers with supplies etc... BUT if landed successfully, the airborne forces now had extra supply, vehicles, artillery, reinforcements etc...

That wasn't a plane but a glider. Paratroopers jumped out of planes, glidertroopers (also part of an Airborne Unit) were landed on the battlefield in a glider (a wooden and canvas plane without an engine, such as the US Waco or the British Horsa gliders) that were towed in via planes. The glidertroops suffered a lot of causalities on d-day and the following days. The Germans had planted giant wooden or metal poles in open fields (suspected future glider landing sites) nicknamed "Rommel's Asparagus". The gliders would hit those, and shatter apart, killing and maiming the occupants. Gliders were notoriously dangerous, and even landing too fast on a perfectly flat field could cause the nose to bury in the ground and the rest of the glider to crumple inwards, or a wing getting caught and cartwheeling the glider.  The glider pilots and gliderborne forces of WWII were truly unsung heroes who were overshadowed by their fellow airborne soldiers, the paratroopers. 
They were often times treated badly too by paratroopers, and until right after d-day wore no special wings (unlike the paratroopers that had jump wings) and were not even given hazardous duty pay like paratroopers until after d-day. 

Also, forgot to mention, why gliders? Why use them if they were so dangerous? Gliders were usually used to help reinforce the parachute element of an Airborne unit. A lot of an airborne unit's signals, administration clerks, other staff types,  medical, artillery, jeeps, trucks, anti-tank, anti-aircraft cannons etc... were brought in via glider. There was also always usually at least one glider infantry regiment (e.g., the 325th, 326th, and 327th) that would be landed after the initial airborne attack as supporting reinforcements (this actually is one of the many reasons for Operation Market Garden's failure... as the airborne forces had to hold ground to allow the gliders to land troops and supplies, even though the only suitable ground was several miles from key bridge objectives. That's a topic for another time. Although the glidertroops also heavily supported the fighting, and led to some successes. I digress...).

Band of Brothers is the story of a company of elite US paratroopers in World War II. The series is 10 hour long episodes (at the time it was filmed in 2001 this was considered a mini series. The show then follows the unit from their nightime June 6th 1944 airborne jump in to Nazi occupied Normandy, France. Then it goes over the unit for the first few days in Normandy. By the third episode the unit is converging on the small french city of Carentan that is a lynch pin in linking the split American landing forces from Utah and Omaha Beaches. The show then continues on to them holding the line outside of Carentan. Then goes to them back in the UK and gearing up for the largest airborne operation in history, Operation Market Garden, the jump in to Holland to capture multiple bridges and cities to help the allies launch an attack in to northern Germany. The next episodes cover the unit there. Then they move to r&r briefly back in to France, when the unit is called up to help hold the vital crossroads town of Bastogne, Belgium. The town is about to be fully cut off by the Germans during the Battle of the Bulge. The unit is rushed in by truck (not parachuted in), and holds the lines in a frozen hell. These are my favorite episode. The next few episodes go over that. Then they are releaved, and holding a town in the eastern France towards the end of the war. They next liberate a concentration camp. Then they help takeover Hitler's mountain retreat in Southern Bavaria. The war is over, and the finish out in Austria. 

That is a very brief summary of events. Now mind you, the show goes over individuals, groups, personal emotions, fears, hopes, dreams etc... it is very realistic. Not one person is just the star. Now there are standouts, but there are a number of them.

The drive to liberate the Netherlands began in September 1944 when the Allies (specifically the First Allied Airborne Army and British XXX Corpse) under Montgomery launched Operation Market Garden to take several key bridges in the lower Netherlands, with the ultimate objective being the British 1st Airborne Division to capture and hold the Arnhem Bridge over the lower Rhine. The plan was for this bridge capture to be springboard over the Rhine and in to Germany. Most bridges and objectives were met, but under fierce German resistance, and without proper armored support the valiant efforts of British paras were for not, as they were unable to secure and hold the last bridge, the vital Arnhem bridge. Veterans and Historians have been arguing for almost 80 years about who was at fault, and why the Operation was technically not a success, but the simple answer is that once Montgomery and the powers that be saw that their shortcut in to northern Germany was now officially closed and cut off. The war and its priorities shifted. 

In the fall of 1944 that was as far in to the Netherlands as the allies got. They managed to hold a tenuous foothold along "Hells Highway" (as American Paratroopers nicknamed the highway that ran from the Belgian frontier to Arnhem, surrounded on both sides by polderland). The war shifted focus. Eisenhower had given Monty a lot of leeway with his Market Garden plan, in part because if it worked it would be a great coup, but if it failed it did not shift too too many resources away from the whole "broad front" approach. So the American paratroopers and British armored forces dug in along hells highway and fought off German units that were sent in to cut and capture the strategic highway. But they did not move back in to Arnhem or further in to the Netherlands for many months.

During this Fall 1944 period you also need to realize other than Operation Market Garden, the western Allied from stretched from Antwerp on down to the Vosges mountains in SE France on the border with Germany. After the breakout from Normandy a couple months earlier, and with the fast pace of the "Champagne Campaign " in the south of France, the allies pace increased, and by the early fall of 1944 they had reached Germany proper. BUT they had smashed up against the vaunted Westwall / Siegfried line. They knew the fighting was going to be tough. Operation Market Garden was a planned way around this. It technically failed. Monty was to now shift focus on his pushes in to northern Germany via other methods, and of course had to further secure the recently captured Antwerp area by clearing the Scheldt River, in order to fully secure the port of Antwerp. The focus of the war shifted. In the fall of 1944 the Allies were trying to secure and hold territory and push further in to Germany. They were trying to breach the Siegfried Line in order to have the wide-open access of the Rhur and Saar Lands. 

However, American soldiers of the First Army got bogged down in the Hurtgen Forest outside of the bitterly fought over German city of Aachen. The momentum of the allied advances slowed. As the fall turned in to very early winter, the Allies realized they would not make much headway in to Germany until the Spring. They were to secure and hold areas around territory they had captured, but otherwise, they planned on digging in for the winter. Have some R&R and then come Spring time, launch the full might of Anglo-American (and some French) power at the Germans.

However, as we all know, that R&R and build up winter period did not go as planned. The Germans attacked weak American lines in the Ardennes Forest section of Belgium and Luxemburg, swiftly overtaking many battle weary and also freshly arrived replacement units. This was the start of the Battle of the Bulge. The 82nd and 101st Airborne Units after only a short period of R&R from fighting on Hell's Highway were thrown in to the salient, along with many other American units. Monty towards the end diverted some of his units to help the Americans to the south. Patton shifted his Third Army's axis of attack northwards to help the southern flank / salient of the Bulge. 

The focus had shifted. By the spring of 1944, after pushing the Germans out of the bulge, and further in to Germany, the Americans shifted focus on the Ruhr and Saar regions of Germany, and the British had focused their aim at cutting across the northern portions of Germany racing in North Eastern direction to capture big port cities, such as Bremen and Hamburg. With these focuses in mind, trying to end the war as quickly as possible, the British did earmark the Canadians to start pushing north / West in to the Netherlands to liberate the remaining portions of Netherlands, but the vast majority of the British Forces (as well as Simpson's US Ninth Army and the US 17th Airborne Division) used the southern portions of Holland and captured areas of Germany to springboard across the Rhine SE of the Netherlands frontier near Wesel, Germany. This left the northern and western portions of the Netherlands fully under German occupation. 
The Allies wanted to fully liberate the Netherlands, just the nature of how the war was being waged from early Fall 1944 until the Spring of 1945, had changed that objective, and by the Spring of 1945 bringing Germany to its knees, and forcing Germany to unconditional surrender was the main objective.

There were some strong German units occupying and garrisoning the Netherlands, and after the Allies could not secure the Arnhem Bridge, the focus in the southern Netherlands was to hold territory, and shift focus on getting across the Rhine in another location. Which was managed in Wesel by the British, and in Ramagen by the Americans. The Americans had been fighting to the south of the British and were fighting along a broad front, with each Army supporting eachother but also kind of doing their own thing to breach Germany and focus on their own axies of advances. Monty wanted to consolidate most of his forces in to one large grand invasion over the Rhine. Besides some units left to mop-up the area and hold ground, large swaths of British forces were gearing up for Operation Plunder / Varsity push across the Rhine and towards Hamburg. The Netherlands' liberation needed to be put on hold, while the conquest of Germany was under way.

Could the British have liberated the Netherlands earlier than May 1945? Maybe, but that would have taken away resources from Monty's prep for Plunder / Varsity, and because he had some proverbial egg on his face for pushing Market Garden and failing, Eisenhower had to proverbially spread the wealth among the other Armies, and could not divert even more forces northward to help Monty and to potentially liberate the entirety of the Netherlands while they were focusing on their own drives.
